title: The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia
subtitle: 1902–today · Ibn Saud's Conquest, the Oil State, the Turn of 1979 and the MBS Transformation

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: The third Saudi state — founded by ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz from the recapture of Riyadh, unified as a kingdom in 1932, made rich by oil, and since 2015 remade under King Salman and his son Mohammed bin Salman

entries.label: ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Ibn Saud)
entries.hint: Aged about 26, ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz retook Riyadh from the Āl Rashīd in January 1902 and spent three decades conquering the peninsula — al-Aḥsāʾ 1913, Ḥāʾil 1921, the Hijaz 1925 — proclaiming the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in 1932. He ruled it, personally, until his death.
entries.note: H. St John Philby, 'Saʿudi Arabia' (1955); Madawi Al-Rasheed, 'A History of Saudi Arabia' (2010); the founding narrative is curated by the King ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz Foundation (Darah).

entries.label: King Saud
entries.hint: ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz's eldest surviving son inherited a state whose oil income he spent faster than it came in, twice bringing it near bankruptcy. After a long power struggle with his brother Faisal, the senior princes and the ʿulamāʾ deposed him in 1964.
entries.note: Al-Rasheed (2010); Sarah Yizraeli, 'Politics and Society in Saudi Arabia' (2012).

entries.label: King Faisal
entries.hint: Faisal abolished slavery (1962), introduced television and state girls' schooling over religious protest, founded the Organisation of the Islamic Conference (1969), and led the 1973 oil embargo. He was shot dead by a nephew in March 1975.
entries.note: Alexei Vassiliev, 'King Faisal of Saudi Arabia' (2012); the OIC founding documents (Rabat, 1969).

entries.label: King Khalid
entries.hint: Khalid's reign was the height of the oil boom and the year of two shocks — the Iranian Revolution and the 1979 seizure of the Grand Mosque — after which the state deliberately deepened its religious conservatism. Crown Prince Fahd ran much of the government.
entries.note: Al-Rasheed (2010); Yaroslav Trofimov, 'The Siege of Mecca' (2007).

entries.label: King Fahd
entries.hint: Fahd took the title Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques (1986), invited US troops to defend the kingdom against Iraq in 1990, and issued the 1992 Basic Law. A stroke in 1995 left Crown Prince Abdullah as de facto ruler for his last decade.
entries.note: the Basic Law of Governance (Royal Order A/90, 1 March 1992); Al-Rasheed (2010).
keywords: Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques

entries.label: King Abdullah
entries.hint: Abdullah pursued cautious reform — the KAUST university (2009), tens of thousands of state scholarships to the West, women on the Consultative Council (2013) and the municipal vote (2015) — while bankrolling the counter-revolution against the 2011 Arab Spring.
entries.note: Al-Rasheed, 'Muted Modernists' (2015); the 2011 royal spending decrees (Umm al-Qura).

entries.label: King Salman
entries.hint: Salman acceded in January 2015 and elevated his son Mohammed bin Salman through the ranks. As of early 2026 he remains king; MBS, as crown prince and prime minister, exercises day-to-day power.
entries.note: the royal succession decrees 2015–2017 (Umm al-Qura); this entry records the position as of early 2026.

entries.label: The pre-oil administration
entries.hint: ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ruled through a handful of advisers — Ḥāfiẓ Wahba, Yūsuf Yāsīn, Fuʾād Ḥamza, the Englishman Philby — with almost no bureaucracy. The Council of Ministers was created only in 1953, days before he died.
entries.note: Philby (1955); the 1953 Council of Ministers decree; Steffen Hertog, 'Princes, Brokers, and Bureaucrats' (2010).

entries.label: The Council of Ministers era
entries.hint: For sixty years the king was prime minister and the crown prince his deputy, with a cabinet of princes and technocrats — Ahmed Zaki Yamani at oil for a generation, the finance and interior ministries as family fiefs — running an oil-funded state that grew enormously.
entries.note: Hertog, 'Princes, Brokers, and Bureaucrats' (2010); the ministerial appointment decrees (Umm al-Qura).

entries.label: Mohammed bin Salman
entries.hint: Deputy crown prince in 2015, crown prince in 2017 after the removal of Muhammad bin Nayef, and prime minister since 2022 — the effective ruler, the author of Vision 2030, and the driver of both the social opening and the political crackdown.
entries.note: the June 2017 succession decree; the September 2022 royal order making the crown prince prime minister (Umm al-Qura).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The wars of unification and the Ikhwān that fought them, the crushing of the Ikhwān when they would not stop, the 1934 war with Yemen, the Grand Mosque siege, an al-Qaeda insurgency, and the wars abroad since 2015

entries.label: The reconquest
entries.loc: Riyadh, al-Qaṣīm and al-Aḥsāʾ, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: From the storming of the al-Musmak fort in Riyadh in January 1902, ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz fought the Āl Rashīd for al-Qaṣīm across a decade, then took al-Aḥsāʾ and the Gulf coast from the Ottomans in 1913 — the core of the future kingdom.
entries.note: Philby (1955); Al-Rasheed (2010).

entries.label: The Ikhwān and the conquests of the 1910s–20s
entries.hint: ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz settled bedouin in indoctrinated agricultural-military colonies (hijar), forming the Ikhwān — a fanatical infantry that became his shock force at Turaba (1919), the taking of Ḥāʾil (1921) and the conquest of the Hijaz.
entries.note: John Habib, 'Ibn Saʿud's Warriors of Islam: The Ikhwan of Najd' (1978); Al-Rasheed (2010).

entries.label: The conquest of the Hijaz and the Baqīʿ demolitions
entries.hint: The Ikhwān sacked Ṭāʾif in 1924, took Mecca, and besieged Jeddah and Medina; Sharif Hussein abdicated. In 1925–26 the tomb-shrines of the Baqīʿ and Muʿallāʾ cemeteries and much of old Mecca and Medina were demolished — a lasting rupture with the wider Muslim world.
entries.note: the contemporary press and the first Muslim World Congress (1926); Al-Rasheed (2010).

entries.label: The Ikhwān revolt and the Battle of Sabilla
entries.hint: The Ikhwān rebelled when ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz halted the jihad at the British-drawn borders, banned raiding and allowed cars and the telegraph. He crushed them at Sabilla in 1929 — the last great camel-cavalry battle — with British aircraft sealing the Iraqi frontier.
entries.note: Habib (1978); the RAF Iraq Command records; the surrender of the leaders in 1930.

entries.label: The war of 1934
entries.hint: A short war with Imam Yahya's Yemen ended with the Treaty of Ṭāʾif, which fixed the southern border and added ʿAsīr, Najrān and Jīzān to the kingdom — provinces Yemen has never fully accepted the loss of.
entries.note: the Treaty of Ṭāʾif, 20 May 1934.

entries.label: The seizure of the Grand Mosque
entries.hint: Juhaymān al-ʿUtaybī and several hundred armed millenarians seized the Grand Mosque in Mecca in November 1979, proclaiming a Mahdi, and held it for two weeks. Hundreds died in the siege; the surviving militants were beheaded. It was a revolt from inside the Wahhābī world.
entries.note: Yaroslav Trofimov, 'The Siege of Mecca' (2007); Thomas Hegghammer and Stéphane Lacroix on Juhaymān.

entries.label: The al-Qaeda insurgency
entries.loc: Riyadh, Yanbuʿ and the Eastern Province
entries.hint: Al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula bombed housing compounds, attacked Western workers and oil facilities, and killed hundreds before the security services broke it — the domestic blowback of the movement that Saudi money and the Afghan jihad had helped create.
entries.note: Thomas Hegghammer, 'Jihad in Saudi Arabia' (2010); the 2003 Riyadh compound bombings.

entries.label: The wars abroad since 2015
entries.loc: Yemen · and targets inside the kingdom
entries.hint: The Saudi-led intervention in Yemen from 2015, the missile and drone attacks on the kingdom in return — including the 2019 Abqaiq–Khurais strike that briefly halved Saudi output — and the Red Sea shipping crisis. As of early 2026 a Yemen truce holds but no settlement.
entries.note: UN Security Council resolutions on Yemen; the September 2019 Abqaiq attack.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The naming of the kingdom, the oil concession and the nationalisation of Aramco, the abolition of slavery, the Basic Law, the reordered succession, and the fiscal turn of Vision 2030

entries.label: The 1932 unification
entries.hint: On 23 September 1932 the Kingdom of the Hijaz and Najd was renamed the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia — the two conquered halves merged under a single name, and that name the ruling family's own. It is the constitutional foundation of the state.
entries.note: the unification decree of 23 September 1932, now the national day.

entries.label: The oil concession and Aramco
entries.hint: The 1933 concession to Standard Oil of California, the 1938 discovery at Dammam No. 7, the growth of the Arabian American Oil Company, and its step-by-step nationalisation, completed in 1980 — the process that turned a bankrupt emirate into an oil state.
entries.note: the 1933 concession agreement; Robert Vitalis, 'America's Kingdom: Mythmaking on the Saudi Oil Frontier' (2007).

entries.label: The abolition of slavery
entries.hint: King Faisal's decree of 1962 ended the legal status of slavery, freeing an enslaved population estimated in the tens of thousands, under long British and then American pressure. It was one of the last states in the world to abolish it.
entries.note: the 1962 abolition decree; Suzanne Miers, 'Slavery in the Twentieth Century' (2003).

entries.label: The Basic Law of Governance
entries.hint: King Fahd's Basic Law defines the kingdom as a monarchy governed by the Qurʾan and the Sunna, with an appointed Consultative Council. It is the nearest thing to a constitution and states explicitly that the Qurʾan and Sunna are the constitution.
entries.note: the Basic Law of Governance (Royal Order A/90, 1 March 1992); the Consultative Council Law of 1992.

entries.label: The reordering of the succession
entries.hint: The 2006 Allegiance Council was meant to regularise the passage of power among ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz's descendants; in 2017 it was effectively bypassed when Mohammed bin Salman replaced Muhammad bin Nayef as crown prince. The third state's dynastic question is unresolved.
entries.note: the Allegiance Institution Law (2006); the June 2017 succession decree.

entries.label: Vision 2030 and the fiscal turn
entries.hint: The 2016 diversification programme, the expansion of the Public Investment Fund, the 2018 introduction of a value-added tax (raised to 15% in 2020) and cuts to fuel and utility subsidies — the beginning of the unwinding of the no-tax rentier bargain.
entries.note: 'Vision 2030' (Council of Economic and Development Affairs, April 2016); the VAT law (2017) and its 2020 amendment.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The Wahhābī establishment as a branch of the state, the deliberate re-Islamisation after 1979, the second-class Shiʿi minority, the Ṣaḥwa and its crushing, and MBS's break with the whole post-1979 order

entries.label: The religious establishment as a state institution
entries.hint: The Āl al-Shaykh and the Council of Senior Scholars were given control of the courts, the mosques, education and the religious police in exchange for legitimising the monarchy — the 1744 pact turned into a bureaucracy.
entries.note: Guido Steinberg, 'Religion und Staat in Saudi-Arabien' (2002); the Council of Senior Scholars, established 1971.

entries.label: The turn after 1979
entries.loc: Saudi Arabia · and the wider Muslim world
entries.hint: The regime's response to the Grand Mosque seizure and the Iranian Revolution was to give the religious establishment more money and reach, tolerate the Ṣaḥwa, and fund missionary work and the Afghan jihad worldwide — two decades of intensified religiosity.
entries.note: Trofimov (2007); Gilles Kepel, 'Jihad' (2002); David Commins, 'The Wahhabi Mission and Saudi Arabia' (2006).

entries.label: The Shiʿi minority
entries.loc: the Eastern Province and Najrān, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: Roughly a tenth of the population, concentrated in the Eastern Province and Najrān, the Shiʿa have faced restricted worship, exclusion from senior posts and periodic unrest — the 1979–80 rising, the 2011–12 protests, and the 2016 execution of the cleric Nimr al-Nimr.
entries.note: Toby Matthiesen, 'The Other Saudis: Shiism, Dissent and Sectarianism' (2015); the January 2016 executions.

entries.label: The Ṣaḥwa and its crushing
entries.loc: the universities and mosques of Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: The Islamist current that grew inside the universities opposed the 1990 arrival of US troops, produced the reform petitions of 1991–92 and a generation of activist clerics such as Salman al-ʿAwda — and was dismantled from 2017, its leading figures jailed.
entries.note: Stéphane Lacroix, 'Awakening Islam: The Politics of Religious Dissent in Contemporary Saudi Arabia' (2011); the September 2017 arrests.

entries.label: State-defined 'moderate Islam'
entries.hint: MBS's public break with the post-1979 order: the religious police stripped of arrest powers (2016), a promised 'moderate Islam open to the world', the clerics sidelined, and the assertion that the state, not the ʿulamāʾ, defines the religion — the deepest revision of the settlement since 1744.
entries.note: the April 2016 decree on the CPVPV; MBS's 2017–2018 public statements; the analysis in Al-Rasheed, 'The Son King' (2020).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: A heritage state built as fast as the old cities are demolished, the rendered mega-projects, Nabaṭī poetry with a royal patron, the cinema and concert opening, and a women's novel written largely from abroad

entries.label: Diriyah, AlUla and the heritage state
entries.hint: The restoration of at-Ṭurayf, the AlUla development around the Nabataean site of Hegra, and the Winter at Tantora festival build a pre-oil national heritage — even as the Haram expansions in Mecca and Medina have demolished most of the two cities' Ottoman and early-Islamic fabric.
entries.note: the Diriyah Gate and Royal Commission for AlUla projects; Sami Angawi and others on the loss of Meccan heritage.

entries.label: The new Riyadh and NEOM
entries.loc: Riyadh and Tabuk Province, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: The Kingdom Centre and the Riyadh skyline, and the rendered mega-projects — NEOM and its linear city, Qiddiya, the Red Sea resorts — are the visual programme of Vision 2030, promoted heavily whether or not they are ever fully built.
entries.note: the NEOM and Vision 2030 project documents; independent reporting on construction progress and cost.

entries.label: Nabaṭī poetry and the royal patron
entries.loc: Riyadh · and the Gulf poetry stage
entries.hint: The vernacular poetry stayed central to public life — the 'Million's Poet' television contest, the standing of poet-princes such as Khalid al-Faisal, and poetry recited at every state and tribal occasion as a still-living political and social medium.
entries.note: Saad Sowayan on Nabaṭī poetry; Marcel Kurpershoek's translations; the 'Million's Poet' (Shāʿir al-Milyūn) format.

entries.label: The cinema and concert opening
entries.hint: Haifaa al-Mansour shot 'Wadjda' (2012) in a country with no cinemas; in 2018 cinemas reopened, the General Entertainment Authority was founded, and concerts, the Red Sea Film Festival and the MDLBEAST music festival followed — a state-driven cultural opening.
entries.note: Haifaa al-Mansour, 'Wadjda' (2012) and 'The Perfect Candidate' (2019); the 2018 lifting of the cinema ban.

entries.label: The Saudi novel
entries.hint: Abd al-Rahman Munif's oil-state epic 'Cities of Salt', Raja Alem (International Prize for Arabic Fiction, 2011), Rajaa al-Sanea's 'Girls of Riyadh' (2005), Mohammed Hasan Alwan — a modern Saudi literature much of it by women and much of it published or set outside the kingdom.
entries.note: the International Prize for Arabic Fiction records; Rajaa al-Sanea, 'Banat al-Riyadh' (2005).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The foreign advisers who wrote the early kingdom, the state history and its revisionists, the guarded science of the oil reserves, and the scholarship generation

entries.label: Philby, Twitchell and the outside experts
entries.loc: Riyadh and the Eastern Province, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: H. St John Philby, the geologist Karl Twitchell and the Aramco Arabists were the early kingdom's window on the outside world and, through their writing, much of the outside world's window on it — advisers, explorers and image-makers at once.
entries.note: Philby, 'The Heart of Arabia' (1922) and 'Saʿudi Arabia' (1955); Vitalis, 'America's Kingdom' (2007) on the Aramco Arabists.

entries.label: The state history and its revisionists
entries.hint: The official history — the founding narrative of ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, the Darah archive, the school curriculum — is answered by a revisionist scholarship (Al-Rasheed, Steinberg, Vitalis, Menoret) that reads the record against the state's account of itself.
entries.note: Al-Rasheed, 'A History of Saudi Arabia' (2010); Pascal Menoret, 'The Saudi Enigma' (2005).

entries.label: The oil-knowledge complex
entries.hint: The geology and engineering of the world's largest conventional reserves, Aramco's technical corps, and the long-running arguments over the true size of the reserves and the sustainability of the Ghawār field — a body of expertise the kingdom holds very close.
entries.note: Matthew Simmons, 'Twilight in the Desert' (2005) and the rebuttals; the Aramco 2019 IPO prospectus reserve disclosures.

entries.label: KAUST and the scholarship generation
entries.hint: The King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (2009), co-educational and secular by design, and the King Abdullah Scholarship Program, which sent tens of thousands of Saudis to Western universities — a deliberate import of outside knowledge and outlook.
entries.note: the KAUST founding charter (2009); the scholarship programme figures from the Ministry of Education.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: A near-bankrupt Hajj economy transformed by oil, the 1973 price weapon, a rentier social contract now under strain, a workforce that is mostly non-citizen, and the Aramco listing and the sovereign fund

entries.label: Before oil — the Hajj and near-bankruptcy
entries.hint: The pre-oil state lived on pilgrimage receipts and British subsidies. The Depression collapsed the Hajj and left ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz unable to pay his men — the desperation that made a speculative oil concession worth signing in 1933.
entries.note: Vitalis, 'America's Kingdom' (2007); Philby (1955).

entries.label: The oil economy
entries.hint: From the first exports in 1939, oil made Saudi Arabia the world's largest crude exporter and the holder of around a sixth of proven reserves. The revenue built the entire modern state — the roads, the cities, the welfare, the army.
entries.note: BP Statistical Review / Energy Institute data; OPEC Annual Statistical Bulletin.

entries.label: The oil weapon and the price shocks
entries.hint: The OPEC embargo of October 1973 quadrupled the oil price and made Saudi Arabia rich and geopolitically central; the 1979–80 second shock deepened it; the 1980s glut and the 1998 price crash showed how exposed a one-commodity economy was.
entries.note: the OPEC records of the October 1973 embargo; Daniel Yergin, 'The Prize' (1991).

entries.label: The rentier social contract
entries.hint: No personal income tax, cradle-to-grave welfare, near-universal public-sector jobs for citizens, cheap fuel and power — the bargain bought with oil money. A young, fast-growing population and lower real oil income have made it increasingly hard to sustain.
entries.note: Hazem Beblawi and Giacomo Luciani on the rentier state; the IMF Article IV consultations on Saudi Arabia.

entries.label: Migrant labour and kafala
entries.hint: Non-citizens are roughly two-fifths of the population and most of the private-sector workforce. The kafala sponsorship system tied a worker to one employer until partial reforms in 2021, and 'Saudization' quotas push citizens into private jobs.
entries.note: the General Authority for Statistics (GASTAT) population and labour data; the March 2021 Labour Reform Initiative.

entries.label: The Aramco listing and the PIF
entries.hint: The December 2019 partial listing of Aramco raised about 25 billion dollars — the largest IPO in history — at a valuation near two trillion. The Public Investment Fund has since become a global sovereign investor, buying football clubs, tech stakes and the mega-projects.
entries.note: the Saudi Aramco IPO prospectus (2019); the PIF annual reports.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: A 32-million-person country living on desalinated and fossil water, the oil plant the world economy leans on, and a heavily surveilled online public

entries.label: Water and the desert kingdom
entries.hint: A 1980s–2000s wheat-subsidy programme drained the fossil aquifers and was then abandoned; the kingdom now has among the world's largest desalination capacities, and a population of over 32 million lives on engineered water.
entries.note: Christopher Ward on Saudi groundwater; the Saline Water Conversion Corporation figures; the 2016 end of the wheat programme.

entries.label: The oil infrastructure
entries.loc: Ghawār, Abqaiq and Ras Tanura, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: Ghawār, the largest conventional oil field ever found; the Abqaiq processing plant, hit by drones and missiles in 2019; Ras Tanura and the refineries; the pipelines and terminals — the physical plant that the global oil market depends on for its spare capacity.
entries.note: the Aramco IPO prospectus; the September 2019 Abqaiq–Khurais attack and its effect on output.

entries.label: Surveillance and the connected kingdom
entries.hint: Saudis are among the world's heaviest social-media users, and the state has invested heavily in monitoring them — the use of Pegasus and other spyware, the 2019 US indictment of two Twitter employees as Saudi agents, and prison sentences of decades for online posts.
entries.note: the Citizen Lab reports on Pegasus targeting; the November 2019 US Department of Justice indictment; the 2022–23 online-speech sentences (Salma al-Shehab and others). NGO monitoring flagged.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: A first British patron, the American oil-for-security bargain, the Arab Cold War against Nasser, the long duel with revolutionary Iran, the 1990 Gulf War and its blowback, and the hedging foreign policy of MBS

entries.label: The Anglo-Saudi relationship
entries.hint: The 1915 Treaty of Darin, the wartime subsidy, the drawing of the borders with Iraq, Transjordan and Kuwait at the 1922 ʿUqayr conference, and the rivalry with the British-backed Hashemites — Britain was the kingdom's first great-power patron.
entries.note: the Treaty of Darin (1915); the ʿUqayr Protocol (1922); Clive Leatherdale, 'Britain and Saudi Arabia 1925–1939' (1983).

entries.label: Quincy and the American alliance
entries.hint: Franklin Roosevelt's meeting with ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz aboard the USS Quincy in February 1945 founded the oil-for-security bargain — US access to Saudi oil and bases, an American guarantee of the kingdom's security — the axis of Saudi foreign policy for seventy years.
entries.note: the State Department record of the Quincy meeting; Rachel Bronson, 'Thicker than Oil' (2006).

entries.label: The Arab Cold War
entries.hint: Saudi Arabia was the conservative pole against Nasser's revolutionary Arabism — funding the monarchies, absorbing the Muslim Brotherhood exiles, and fighting a proxy war against Egypt in the North Yemen civil war of 1962–70.
entries.note: Malcolm Kerr, 'The Arab Cold War' (1971); Jesse Ferris, 'Nasser's Gamble' (2013).

entries.label: The duel with revolutionary Iran
entries.hint: Since 1979 the Islamic Republic has been the kingdom's defining regional adversary — over the Gulf, Lebanon, Syria, Iraq, Yemen and the leadership of the Muslim world. A China-brokered resumption of diplomatic relations in March 2023 cooled but did not end it.
entries.note: the March 2023 Beijing agreement; F. Gregory Gause, 'Saudi Arabia's Regional Security Strategy'.

entries.label: The Gulf War and its blowback
entries.loc: Saudi Arabia · Kuwait · New York and Washington
entries.hint: The invitation of some half a million US troops to defend the kingdom against Iraq in 1990 was denounced by the Islamists as the defilement of the land of the Ḥaramayn — the specific grievance behind al-Qaeda and the September 11 attacks, fifteen of whose nineteen hijackers were Saudi citizens.
entries.note: the 9/11 Commission Report (2004); Steve Coll, 'The Bin Ladens' (2008).

entries.label: The MBS foreign policy
entries.hint: The Yemen war, the 2017–21 blockade of Qatar, the 2018 killing of Jamal Khashoggi and its diplomatic cost, a hedging away from Washington through OPEC+ oil cuts with Russia, the paused Israel normalisation talks, and the sport and Expo diplomacy — a more independent and transactional posture.
entries.note: the 2021 Al-Ula reconciliation with Qatar; the 2021 US ODNI assessment on the Khashoggi killing; reporting on OPEC+ 2022–2025.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The Saudi state that finally lasted, the oil superpower and custodian of Islam's holiest places, 1979 as the hinge of its religious turn, and the still-open MBS transformation

entries.label: The state that lasted
entries.hint: The third Saudi state solved what destroyed the first two — succession fixed within one family, finance from oil instead of plunder, and the doctrine controlled by the state rather than the ʿulamāʾ or the Ikhwān. It is the longest-lived Arabian state since the early Caliphate.
entries.note: Al-Rasheed, 'A History of Saudi Arabia' (2010); the comparison to the first two states is the historiography's own.

entries.label: The oil superpower and the custodian of Islam
entries.loc: Riyadh, Mecca and the Eastern Province
entries.hint: From a near-bankrupt desert emirate, the kingdom became the holder of the world's swing oil capacity, the guardian of Mecca and Medina, and the financier of a worldwide religious network — an outsized weight for a country of its population.
entries.note: Bronson, 'Thicker than Oil' (2006); Commins, 'The Wahhabi Mission' (2006).

entries.label: 1979 as the hinge
entries.hint: The Grand Mosque seizure, the Iranian Revolution and the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan together pushed the kingdom into two decades of intensified religious conservatism and global daʿwa — the world Osama bin Laden emerged from, and the world MBS is now trying to undo.
entries.note: Trofimov (2007); Kepel, 'Jihad' (2002).

entries.label: The MBS transformation, outcome open
entries.hint: Since 2016 the kingdom has attempted the deepest change to its social and religious order since 1744 — women driving, cinemas, the clerics sidelined, the economy rebuilt around a sovereign fund — while tightening political control and jailing critics. As of early 2026 the transformation is well advanced and its durability untested.
entries.note: Al-Rasheed, 'The Son King: Reforming Saudi Arabia' (2020). This entry records the situation as of early 2026 and makes no prediction.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: The century-long arc of women from seclusion to the driving reform, the activists jailed for demanding it, the legacy of abolition, the migrant workforce, and the cost of dissent

entries.label: Women, from seclusion to the driving reform
entries.hint: Girls' state schools opened over protest in 1960; the guardianship system governed adult women's lives; the driving ban was protested in 1990 and 2011 and lifted by royal order in June 2018. Guardianship rules were loosened in 2019 and 2021, and women's workforce participation roughly doubled under Vision 2030.
entries.note: the Royal Order of 26 September 2017 ending the driving ban (effective 24 June 2018); the 2019 travel and civil-status reforms; GASTAT labour-force data.

entries.label: The jailed activists
entries.hint: Loujain al-Hathloul, Samar Badawi, Nassima al-Sadah and others were detained in May 2018 — several reporting torture in custody — for campaigning for the reforms the state then enacted, days before the driving ban was lifted. The message was that change is the state's gift, not a claim to be pressed.
entries.note: the reports of the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention; Amnesty International and HRW documentation (advocacy sources, flagged); al-Hathloul's release in February 2021.

entries.label: The end of slavery and its legacy
entries.hint: The 1962 decree freed an enslaved population; their descendants, and the older questions of colour and status in Saudi society, remain very little discussed in public. The abolition is recorded as a modernising milestone and its human aftermath largely is not.
entries.note: Miers, 'Slavery in the Twentieth Century' (2003); the general silence noted by Al-Rasheed and others.

entries.label: The migrant workforce
entries.hint: The domestic workers, construction labourers and service staff who build and run the kingdom, under a sponsorship system that has left many exposed to non-payment, passport confiscation and abuse. The mega-projects have drawn scrutiny over worker deaths and the pace of the promised reforms.
entries.note: the ILO reporting on the 2021 labour reforms; HRW and ITUC documentation on the mega-projects (advocacy sources, flagged).

entries.label: Dissent and its cost
entries.hint: Saudi Arabia is among the world's leading executioners — 81 people put to death in a single day in March 2022 — with decades-long sentences for online speech and the 2018 killing of the journalist Jamal Khashoggi in the Istanbul consulate, assessed by a UN special rapporteur and US intelligence as a state operation.
entries.note: the report of the UN Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial executions (Agnès Callamard, 2019); the 2021 US ODNI assessment; Amnesty International's annual execution figures (NGO data, flagged).
